critical.claim: ethnicity and athlete type did not affect scores
critical.source_says: Results/Table 6: 'statistically significant difference ... among NCAA, Club, and Intramural athletes' (F(2,277)=8.111, p<.001); NCAA athletes reported significantly less interference. (The paper's abstract states the opposite, but the reported analysis contradicts it.)

minor.issue: No statistics given (ICC 0.74, r=.217 with SCL-90-R, r=.255 with 30-day TLFB, r=.185 with age).

Omits that all participants had to report alcohol or non-prescribed drug use in the prior four months and were referred for performance-optimization programming, which limits the population; omits single Division 1 university and named instruments (SCL-90-R, TLFB, SCID).
Advice on sleep, mood, recovery and separating care from discipline is not derived from the study.
Clinical readiness criteria are generic and not from the source; the study did not address return to sport.

Wording implies the structured clinical interview was given to all 285; the source places the diagnostic measure in the second battery completed by the 74-person subsample. Also omits the inclusion requirement of substance use in the prior four months.
Omits the significant positive correlation with age (r=.185) and does not flag that the abstract's claim of no athlete-type effect conflicts with the reported results.

note: B reports the psychometric statistics and correctly states that NCAA athletes scored lower than club and intramural athletes, whereas A repeats the abstract's contradicted claim that athlete type had no effect and fills practical fields with unsourced advice.
